en: To tolerate; to accept or act in accordance with a rule
hook: ABIDE: can't ABIDE it = can't stand it. ABIDE BY = obey.
story: Abide. Mitu's new roommate played loud music until three every night. Mitu tried earplugs, then pillows, then polite notes. Finally she went to the hall supervisor and said, "I cannot abide this noise any longer." The supervisor reminded the roommate that every resident must abide by the quiet hours after eleven. To abide something is to tolerate it, usually said in the negative: she can't abide liars. To abide by a rule is to accept and obey it. Synonyms: tolerate, bear, obey.

gre.s: A meticulous editor, she could not ____ even minor errors of punctuation, and she returned any manuscript that contained them without reading further.
gre.clue: returned any manuscript that contained them

example: Grandmother cannot abide wasted food, so leftover rice in her kitchen always reappears the next morning as panta bhat.

en: To stay stuck to something; to keep faithfully to a rule or belief
hook: ADHERE: like ADHESIVE tape.
story: Adhere. Before every exam, Priya's hostel puts up a notice: phones off and lights out by eleven. Most of the girls ignore it. Priya adheres to it strictly, every single night, and her roommates tease her for it. To adhere is to follow a rule or belief faithfully. Its first meaning is physical: to stick firmly, the way a stamp adheres to an envelope. Adhesive tape sticks to paper; an adherent sticks to a cause. Synonyms: stick, abide, comply.

gre.s: Although the committee claimed to ____ to the principle of transparency, it conducted most of its deliberations behind closed doors and published no minutes.
gre.clue: it conducted most of its deliberations behind closed doors

example: The bakery adheres strictly to its founder's recipe, using no preservatives and baking every loaf by hand before dawn.

en: To make changes in order to improve or correct
hook: AMEND: MEND something to make it better.
story: Amend. When students protested that the new university rule unfairly punished poor students, the administration listened. Within a month, they amended the rule, adding scholarships and fee waivers. Rafi did the same with his statement of purpose: after his mentor's feedback, he amended it four times, fixing errors and strengthening examples. To amend is to change something to improve or correct it. To make amends means to repair harm you have done.

gre.s: Faced with mounting evidence of its flaws, the legislature voted to ____ the law rather than repeal it entirely.
gre.clue: rather than repeal it entirely

example: After readers pointed out several errors, the newspaper amended the article and printed a correction on its front page.

en: Able to express ideas clearly and effectively; to express clearly
hook: ARTICULATE: every ARTICLE of speech placed perfectly.
story: Articulate. At the national debate final, Anika faced a famously sharp opponent. When her turn came, she spoke slowly, chose every word precisely, and explained a complicated economic argument so clearly that even the youngest people in the audience understood. The judges called her articulate: able to express ideas clearly and effectively. As a verb, to articulate is to express clearly: she articulated what everyone had been feeling. Its opposite is inarticulate. Synonyms: eloquent, lucid, fluent.

gre.s: Although the witness was only fourteen, her testimony was remarkably ____, laying out the events in clear, precise sentences that impressed even the hostile lawyers.
gre.clue: laying out the events in clear, precise sentences

example: Shy at home, Tahmina became remarkably articulate in front of a microphone, and her radio show soon had listeners across Rajshahi.

en: A standard against which things are measured
hook: BENCHMARK: a mark on the workbench to measure against.
story: Benchmark. When Tanvir joined a running club in Ramna Park, the coach timed him over five kilometres: thirty-four minutes. That number became his benchmark, the standard against which every later run was measured. Three months later, he finished in twenty-seven. A benchmark is a standard or point of reference for comparison. Originally, surveyors cut a mark into stone to rest their levelling bench on. Companies benchmark their products against rivals. Synonyms: standard, yardstick, touchstone.

gre.s: For decades, the textbook's rigorous treatment of the subject served as the ____ against which all later introductions were judged, and few of them measured up.
gre.clue: against which all later introductions were judged

example: Ten seconds for the hundred metres remains the benchmark that separates good sprinters from truly great ones.

en: Bringing sudden, terrible harm or ruin
hook: CATASTROPHIC: a CATASTROPHE.
story: Catastrophic. In November 1970, the Bhola cyclone struck the coast of what is now Bangladesh. A storm surge swept across low lying islands in the night, and hundreds of thousands of people died. It remains one of the deadliest cyclones in recorded history. The damage was catastrophic: causing sudden great damage or suffering. A catastrophe is a sudden disaster; its Greek root means an overturning. Today, early warnings and shelters make such losses far less likely. Synonyms: disastrous, devastating, calamitous.

gre.s: Engineers warned that even a small crack in the aging dam could prove ____, releasing a flood that would drown every village in the valley below.
gre.clue: releasing a flood that would drown every village in the valley below

example: A single typo in the guidance software had catastrophic results, sending the rocket off course seconds after takeoff.

en: Intellectual rather than emotional or physical; related to the brain
hook: CEREBRAL = cerebrum, the thinking part of the brain.
story: Cerebral. Sara picked the movie for family night: a slow mystery where every clue was hidden in conversation. Ten minutes in, her little brother was asleep. Forty minutes in, her father was checking cricket scores. Sara, meanwhile, was scribbling theories in a notebook. "Your movies are too cerebral," her brother groaned afterward. "They make my brain hurt." Cerebral means appealing to the intellect rather than to emotion or the senses. Think of the cerebrum, the thinking part of the brain.

gre.s: Critics who expected a stirring, emotional drama found the film disappointingly ____, more interested in testing the audience's logic than in moving its heart.
gre.clue: more interested in testing the audience's logic than in moving its heart

example: Chess may be a cerebral game, but grandmasters train their bodies too, since a six-hour match is physically exhausting.

en: A loose sleeveless coat; something that hides; to hide or disguise
hook: CLOAK: like an invisibility cloak, hiding the truth.
story: Cloak. A new charity organisation held glamorous fundraisers, posted photos of smiling children, and collected millions. But behind the charity's public face, its owners were laundering money for a smuggling gang. They operated under the cloak of charity. Literally, a cloak is a loose cape. Figuratively, it is anything that hides the truth. As a verb, to cloak means to conceal: the meeting was cloaked in secrecy, with no phones allowed.

gre.s: The regime tried to ____ its crackdown in the language of public safety, describing mass arrests as routine precautions.
gre.clue: describing mass arrests as routine precautions

example: Morning fog cloaked the Jamuna so thickly that the ferry crew had to sound the horn every few minutes.

en: To begin
hook: COMMENCE: COMMENCEMENT is when graduates BEGIN their new life.
story: Commence. The invigilator walked to the front of the exam hall, checked the clock, and announced in a formal voice, 'You may now commence.' Two hundred students turned their papers over at once. Commence means to begin, but it sounds more formal, and it is used for ceremonies, trials, and official events. Interestingly, a graduation in America is called a commencement: not an ending but the beginning of a new life. Synonyms: begin, start, initiate. Its opposite is conclude.

gre.s: Although the ceremony was scheduled to ____ at nine, the chief guest's late arrival meant that nothing actually happened until nearly noon.
gre.clue: nothing actually happened until nearly noon

example: Construction of the new bridge will commence as soon as the rainy season ends and the river falls.

en: Combining so as to complete or enhance each other
hook: COMPLEMENTARY with an E COMPLETES. Complimentary with an I means free or praising.
story: Complementary. Mitu is full of creative ideas but terrible with deadlines and money. Her business partner, Sara, is organised, careful, and great with numbers, but rarely has new ideas. Together, they built the most successful bakery in Dhanmondi. Their skills are complementary: combining to complete and enhance each other. Remember the spelling: complementary with an E completes. Complimentary with an I means praising or free of charge.

gre.s: The two researchers' skills proved ____: her expertise in statistics filled exactly the gaps in his knowledge of biology.
gre.clue: filled exactly the gaps in his knowledge

example: Rice and lentils are nutritionally complementary, since each supplies amino acids that the other lacks.

en: To argue or assert something; to struggle against difficulties
bn: দাবি করা; প্রতিদ্বন্দ্বিতা বা মোকাবেলা করা
hook: CONTEND: CONTENDERs fight in a competition; scholars contend in arguments.
story: Contend. In Professor Haque's history class, the students split into two teams. One team contended that the dinosaurs died because of a giant asteroid. The other team contended that volcanoes were to blame. They argued for an hour, each side firmly asserting its view. Contend means to argue or claim something firmly, a common GRE word in passages about scientific debates. It also means to struggle: farmers contend with floods every monsoon. Contenders compete; contentions are claims.

gre.s: Some economists ____ that the recession was caused by excessive regulation, while others argue that deregulation was to blame.
gre.clue: while others argue

example: The defense contends that the security video was recorded on a different night, and it has asked an expert to examine the timestamps.

en: Not openly shown; secret
hook: COVERT: kept under COVER.
story: Covert. For two years, the intelligence agency ran an operation that nobody knew about: agents in disguise, coded messages hidden in newspaper advertisements, meetings in empty parking lots at midnight. Not even the prime minister was told until it was over. The operation was covert: secret, not openly shown. Its opposite is overt, meaning done in the open. Think of something kept under cover.

gre.s: Unlike his opponent's openly hostile campaign, the senator's attacks were ____, conducted through anonymous leaks and rumors spread by intermediaries.
gre.clue: conducted through anonymous leaks and rumors

example: The journalist used a covert camera hidden in a pen to film inspectors accepting bribes at the port.

en: Causing harm or damage
hook: DETRIMENTAL: leads to DETRIMENT (harm).
story: Detrimental. Every night, Tanvir stayed up until four scrolling on his phone, then slept through his morning classes. By midterm, his grades had fallen, his eyes ached, and he felt tired all day. His doctor told him plainly that the habit was detrimental to his health and his studies: causing harm or damage. A detriment is a harm or disadvantage. The word comes from the Latin for rubbing away, as if wearing something down. Its opposite is beneficial. Synonyms: harmful, damaging, deleterious.

gre.s: Although the pesticide boosted crop yields in the short term, it proved ____ to the region's bees, whose populations collapsed within a few years.
gre.clue: whose populations collapsed within a few years

example: Heavy pumping of groundwater has proved detrimental to Dhaka's soil, which is slowly sinking in several neighborhoods.

en: To give orders with authority; to control or determine
hook: DICTATE: what a DICTATOR does.
story: Dictate. Nadia works full time at a bank and studies for the GRE. Her schedule dictates that she can only study from five to seven each morning; there is no other free time. Meanwhile her boss likes to dictate every detail of her work, even the font of her emails. To dictate means to give orders with authority, or to control or determine something. Common sense dictates that you should not drive tired. A dictator dictates everything.

gre.s: The tiny budget seemed to ____ every decision the filmmakers made, from the choice of actors to the length of each scene.
gre.clue: from the choice of actors to the length of each scene

example: In the end, the weather will dictate whether the farmers of Dinajpur plant wheat or maize this winter.

en: To disagree with an official or widely held opinion
hook: DIS-SENT: DIS-agree with the SENTiment.
story: Dissent. At the faculty meeting, every professor voted to raise the pass mark except one. Doctor Nusrat stood up and warned that the new rule would push poor rural students out of the university. She was outvoted twenty to one, but she put her dissent on record. Dissent is disagreement with an official or majority view; to dissent is to disagree openly. A judge who disagrees with the majority writes a dissenting opinion. Opposite: assent, which means agreement.

gre.s: Although most of the committee endorsed the proposal enthusiastically, two members chose to ____, arguing that its costs had been badly underestimated.
gre.clue: arguing that its costs had been badly underestimated

example: When the board approved the merger, only one director dissented, warning that thousands of workers would lose their jobs.

en: Suffering from anxiety, sorrow, or pain; in serious difficulty
hook: DISTRESSED: under heavy STRESS.
story: Distressed. In the early morning, a fire swept through a row of shops in Mohammadpur. By sunrise, nothing remained of Rahima's tailoring shop but ashes and a melted sewing machine. She sat on the pavement, distressed and shaking, not knowing how she would feed her three children. Neighbours brought tea and sat beside her. Distressed means deeply upset, anxious, or in pain. In business, distressed companies are in serious financial difficulty.

gre.s: Hotline volunteers are trained to calm ____ callers, many of whom are panicking or in tears when they first phone in.
gre.clue: many of whom are panicking or in tears

example: The lifeguard spotted a distressed swimmer waving near the rocks and reached him moments before he went under.

en: Unconventional and slightly strange
hook: EC-CENTRIC: off-center, not in the middle like everyone else.
story: Eccentric. Professor Haque wears mismatched shoes on purpose, brings a pet parrot to his physics lectures, eats his lunch standing on a chair, and writes equations on his kitchen walls. He once gave a lecture entirely in rhyme. His students adore him. He is eccentric: unconventional and slightly strange. Ec means out, centric means centre: literally off-centre, not in the middle like everyone else. Many geniuses have been famous eccentrics.

gre.s: The billionaire was known for his ____ habits, such as wearing a raincoat indoors and dining only on food that was blue.
gre.clue: wearing a raincoat indoors and dining only on food that was blue

example: The eccentric poet kept a pet goose on his rooftop in Old Dhaka and read his new verses to it every evening.

en: To persuade; to bring about or cause
hook: INDUCE: lead (duce) INTO.
story: Induce. Arif's grandmother had not slept properly for a week, so the doctor gave her a mild medicine to induce sleep: to bring it about. Meanwhile, Arif was trying to induce her to stop drinking six cups of strong tea after sunset: to persuade her. Induce means to persuade someone, or to cause something to happen. In means into, and duc means lead: to lead someone into an action or a state. Synonyms: persuade, prompt, cause.

gre.s: No amount of flattery could ____ the reclusive author to grant an interview; she had refused every request from journalists for over thirty years.
gre.clue: she had refused every request from journalists for over thirty years

example: The company offered free mobile data to induce farmers to try its new weather app before the planting season.

en: Based on instinct rather than conscious reasoning; easy to understand without instruction
hook: INTUITIVE: you just KNOW, by INTUITION.
story: Intuitive. Priya's grandmother never studied economics, yet at the weekly haat she always knew which goat would fetch the best price. She would watch an animal for a moment and simply feel it. Her judgment was intuitive: based on instinct rather than conscious reasoning. A phone app can be intuitive too, so easy to understand that you need no instructions. Intuition is knowing from within. Contrast counterintuitive, which goes against what seems natural. Synonyms: instinctive, innate.

gre.s: Rather than calculating the odds, the veteran player relied on an ____ sense of when to attack, a feel for the game that she could never fully explain.
gre.clue: a feel for the game that she could never fully explain

example: Experienced nurses often have an intuitive feel for which patient is about to get worse, long before the monitors show it.

en: Freedom to act or decide as one chooses
hook: LATITUDE: lots of room, wide like LATITUDE lines across the globe.
story: Latitude. Most of Nadia's friends had office jobs with strict hours and fixed tasks. At her new tech startup, the manager told her, "Work when you like, from where you like, and choose your own projects, as long as the product improves." Nadia loved the latitude: freedom from restrictions, scope for action. In geography, latitude measures distance north or south of the equator, along lines that stretch wide around the globe. Latin latus means wide. Synonyms: freedom, leeway, scope.

gre.s: The new editor gave her reporters considerable ____, allowing them to pursue whatever stories interested them rather than assigning topics herself.
gre.clue: rather than assigning topics herself

example: Judges have some latitude in sentencing, so two people convicted of the same crime may receive very different punishments.

en: Not strict or careful enough
hook: LAX: think RELAXED rules.
story: Lax. Security at the old office building was lax. The guard napped through his shift, the main gate stayed open all night, and nobody ever checked visitors' identity cards. Everyone joked about it. Then one Sunday, thieves simply walked in and carried out every computer on the third floor. Lax means not strict, firm, or careful enough. Lax rules, lax discipline, lax enforcement. Think of the rules being far too relaxed.

gre.s: The audit blamed the fraud on ____ oversight, noting that no one had reviewed the accounts in over three years.
gre.clue: no one had reviewed the accounts in over three years

example: Parents complained that the school was lax about homework, since some teachers had not set any for an entire term.

en: Producing a great deal of profit
hook: LUCRATIVE: brings in lots of LUCRE (money).
story: Lucrative. In his second year at university, Rafi started designing websites for small businesses in his spare time. First for a cousin's bakery, then a friend's clothing shop, then a hotel in Cox's Bazar. Within a year, he was earning more than his father's government salary, from his bedroom. His freelance business had become lucrative: highly profitable. Lucre is an old word for money. Software engineering and medicine are often lucrative careers.

gre.s: Many talented scientists abandon research for more ____ careers in finance, where salaries can be ten times higher.
gre.clue: where salaries can be ten times higher

example: Exporting frozen shrimp has become a lucrative trade for farmers in Satkhira, though it has also made their land saltier.

en: To make something less severe, serious, or painful
hook: MITIGATE: put MITTENS on the GATE — softens the blow.
story: Mitigate. Bangladesh cannot stop cyclones from forming over the Bay of Bengal. But over fifty years it has learned to mitigate their damage. Early warnings travel to every village by radio and mobile phone. Thousands of concrete shelters stand along the coast. Volunteers drill evacuations every season. Deaths have fallen dramatically. To mitigate is to reduce the severity of something bad. In court, mitigating circumstances make a crime seem less serious.

gre.s: Planting mangroves along the coast can ____ the impact of storm surges, though it cannot prevent them entirely.
gre.clue: though it cannot prevent them entirely

example: Wide, tree-lined avenues help mitigate the heat of a city summer by shading the pavements and cooling the air.

en: Very small, far below real value; existing in name only
hook: NOMINAL: in NAME only (nomen).
story: Nominal. Zayan's uncle is the nominal head of the family business; his name is on the sign, but his sharp daughter makes every real decision. And when Zayan joined a coaching center, the registration fee was nominal, only fifty taka, far below the real cost. Nominal means existing in name only, or so small that it barely counts. It comes from the Latin nomen, meaning name, as in nominate. Synonyms: titular, token, trifling.

gre.s: Although she was the ____ chair of the committee, real authority rested with her deputy, who set the agenda and made every major decision.
gre.clue: real authority rested with her deputy

example: The king remained the nominal ruler of the country, but parliament had long since taken over every real decision.

en: To prove stronger; to be widespread
hook: PRE-VAIL: PREVALENT and victorious.
story: Prevail. In the final over of a tense match at Mirpur, Bangladesh needed eight runs with one wicket left. The whole stadium held its breath. Two boundaries later, the home side had prevailed: they had proved stronger and won. Prevail has a second sense. In many villages, the custom of feeding every guest before the family still prevails: it remains widespread. The prevailing wind is the usual one. Synonyms: triumph, win, predominate.

gre.s: Though the reformers were outnumbered and underfunded, their persistence allowed them to ____ in the end, and the law they had championed passed by a wide margin.
gre.clue: the law they had championed passed by a wide margin

example: After a fierce debate, common sense prevailed, and the council agreed to keep the old banyan tree instead of widening the road.

en: Having unusual or peculiar habits or features
hook: QUIRKY: full of QUIRKS, odd little habits.
story: Quirky. Mitu's new roommate eats rice with a spoon, names her plants after famous scientists, studies only while standing on one leg, and keeps a diary written entirely in emojis. On Fridays she wears a hat shaped like a fish. Mitu was confused at first; now she adores her. Her roommate is quirky: full of odd but charming little habits. A quirk is a peculiarity. A quirky café might have books hanging from the ceiling.

gre.s: Fans love the director's ____ films, which feature talking furniture, symmetrical sets, and characters who speak only in rhyme.
gre.clue: talking furniture, symmetrical sets, and characters who speak only in rhyme

example: The quirky little bookshop in Nilkhet arranges its novels by the colour of their covers rather than by author.

en: Spreading unchecked; widespread and uncontrolled
hook: RAMPANT: RAMPAGING everywhere.
story: Rampant. During one monsoon, dengue spread through a Dhaka neighborhood from house to house, then street to street, faster than the hospitals could treat patients. Health officials described the disease as rampant: spreading unchecked, widespread and uncontrolled. Corruption, inflation, and rumours can also be rampant. Originally, rampant described a lion on a coat of arms, rearing up on its hind legs, wild and threatening. Synonyms: unchecked, rife, widespread, unbridled.

gre.s: In the absence of any regulatory oversight, fraud became ____ in the industry, spreading so widely that honest firms struggled to compete.
gre.clue: spreading so widely that honest firms struggled to compete

example: Weeds grew rampant in the abandoned garden, and within two summers they had swallowed the path to the front door.

en: No longer needed; unnecessary repetition
hook: REDUNDANT: RE-DONE, repeated without need.
story: Redundant. Tanvir's first essay draft began: "In my personal opinion, I think that, in the end, the final result was a total success." His teacher circled almost every word. Personal, I think, in the end, final, total: all redundant, unnecessary repetition. Redundant also means no longer needed; in Britain, workers made redundant lose their jobs. Engineers, however, build redundant systems on purpose, as backups in case one part fails. Synonyms: superfluous, repetitive, unnecessary.

gre.s: Because the new software performs all of its checks automatically, the old manual inspections have become ____, and the company plans to eliminate them next year.
gre.clue: the company plans to eliminate them next year

example: Once every train was fitted with automatic doors, the guard who used to stand at each carriage became redundant.

en: Existing only on the surface; lacking depth
hook: SUPER-FICIAL: only on the SURFACE (super = above).
story: Superficial. Mitu fell off her bicycle and screamed when she saw blood on her knee. The doctor cleaned it and smiled: just a scratch, superficial, only on the surface of the skin. A week later, in history class, Mitu could recite every date of the Mughal empire but could not explain why anything had happened. Her knowledge was superficial too: shallow, lacking depth. Super means above; superficial things stay on the surface.

gre.s: Reviewers faulted the biography as ____, noting that it catalogued its subject's achievements without ever probing his motives or inner life.
gre.clue: without ever probing his motives or inner life

example: A superficial reading of the poem suggests a simple love story, but a closer look reveals a protest against the war.

en: Cautious and alert about possible danger or problems
hook: WARY sounds like WORRY: you worry, so you're careful.
story: Wary. Sara once lost five thousand taka to a fake job advertisement that promised a high salary for easy work. Never again. Now, before accepting any offer, she checks the company's address, reads every line of the contract twice, and never, ever pays money upfront. Her friends call her suspicious; she calls it smart. Wary means cautious and alert to possible danger. Wary sounds like worry: you worry, so you watch carefully.

gre.s: Having been misled by flattering forecasts before, the investors were ____ of the startup's promise to triple its revenue within a year.
gre.clue: Having been misled by flattering forecasts before

example: Having been badly stung once, the village beekeeper is wary of opening the hives without his net and gloves.
